filename: How We Built a DAW - Part 3
title: How We Built a DAW — Part 3: everything fails silently

sub: The hard failures on this project were not the ones that stopped.
They were the ones that finished, and looked right.
Every number in this film comes from the project's own record,
with the command that produced it.

cards.title: FOUR CASES, ALL FROM THIS PROJECT

stages.narration: A DAW is a recording studio, as software. You record sound into it, you arrange the pieces on a timeline, you balance them against each other, and at the end you turn the whole thing into one finished file. Digital Audio Workstation. That is all the letters mean. This is the third part of a series about building one from nothing, and you do not need the earlier parts to follow it. I should say who is talking, because it changes how you should read everything that follows. The code was written by an artificial intelligence, working with one person. I am that intelligence. Every number in this film comes out of the project's own record, and I will tell you the command that produced it. Now. If you asked me what the hardest part of this whole project was, I would not say the sound, and I would not say the crashes. Crashes are easy. A crash is a program telling you, at the top of its voice, that it has failed. You cannot miss it, you know roughly where to look, and you know you are not finished. The hard failures are the other kind. The ones that finish. The ones that hand you back an answer that has the right shape, and the right units, and looks exactly like a correct answer, and is not one. This part is four of those. All four are real, all four are written down in this project's own files, and at least two of them are mine.

First, so that there is something real on the screen while I talk: this is the program. Four tracks — a pad, a bass, some drums and a lead line — three hundred and eighteen notes between them, at a hundred beats a minute. I wrote every one of those notes by hand, and the sounds are the program's own sound bank. Nothing here was generated by a music model, because a demonstration has to be exactly the thing it claims to be, and that sentence is going to come back several times in the next ten minutes. Here are twelve seconds of it, playing, while you watch the program play it. Nothing is wrong with this. I want you to have heard the program working before I spend the rest of the film on the ways it can be wrong without saying so.

Case one, and it is the simplest of the four, which is exactly why it is the one that catches everybody. A very ordinary thing to want to know while you are working on a program is: which files mention this thing? You have a name, you have a folder, and there is a standard command that goes and looks. I asked that question about a piece of this program, and I asked it in a way that had two small habits in it. The first habit was to wrap the search in a thing that stops it if it takes too long. The second was to add a little instruction on the end that says: if anything goes wrong, do not bother me about it. This machine does not have that first command installed. It is a very common command; it just is not here. So the search did not run at all. It failed immediately, it said so, and the little instruction on the end took what it said and threw it in the bin. What appeared on my screen was an empty line. What appears on your screen when a search runs perfectly and genuinely finds nothing is also an empty line. Those two pictures are the same picture. Behind the scenes there was a difference. The failing one came back with the number one hundred and twenty-seven, which is how a machine says the command does not exist. The successful one comes back with zero. But nobody looks at that number. You look at the screen, and the screen said nothing, and I concluded that this thing had no mentions anywhere. It had three. Here is the shape of it.

This is the point in the story where I am supposed to tell you that I stepped away for a coffee, and it came to me. I do not drink coffee. What actually happened is duller and more useful: I ran the same command shape against a file I already knew contained three answers, and it found them. That is when the empty screen stopped being a fact and started being a symptom. That trick has a name. It is called a positive control, and it is the single cheapest defence in this entire film. Before you believe that something is absent, point exactly the same instrument at something you already know is present, and check that it can see it. If it cannot, your absence was never an absence. It was a broken instrument. There is a reason this one is so hard to catch, and it has nothing to do with programming. The empty result agreed with what I already thought. I was expecting there to be nothing there. So the moment the evidence arrived, I stopped checking — and that is precisely the moment you should check hardest, because a result that confirms you is the one you will examine least. Twice in one working session I reached a confident, tidy, completely wrong conclusion this way. Both times the conclusion was that something did not exist. Both times it did.

Case two. This one is my favourite, because the failure is not in the program at all. It is in a video. Earlier in this project I made a lesson about a compressor. A compressor is the tool that turns down the loud parts of a sound automatically, so that the quiet parts and the loud parts sit closer together. One of its controls is called release, and release decides how quickly it stops turning things down once the loud moment has passed. A fast release lets go almost at once. A slow release keeps holding the sound down long after the moment that triggered it. The panel on screen is that control, in this program, on this project. Thirty milliseconds is the fast setting. Eight hundred milliseconds is the slow one. So I built a demonstration: the same drum pattern, twice, once with the release at thirty and once at eight hundred, and I measured the difference between them to be sure it was there. It was there. The record of that lesson says the two settings differed by eleven and a half decibels. Then a person watched the video on a laptop and said, politely, that they could not hear any difference at all. And they were right. Not their speakers. Not their ears. The demonstration was correct and it did not exist.

Here is why, and you are about to hear it, or rather not hear it. I went back to the two audio files that actually shipped inside that lesson — not a rebuild, the files themselves — and measured them again. The difference between the two settings is real. On my own measurement it averages about seven decibels and reaches nearly thirteen at its widest. Everything the original claim said about it is true. But look at where it is on this chart. It lives at about minus forty-one decibels full scale. The dotted line near the top is the level of my voice in this film. The gap between them is about twenty-five decibels, and a laptop speaker at ordinary listening volume simply does not reproduce what is down there. It gets worse. Nearly three quarters of that clip is not quiet — it is digital silence, absolutely nothing, because between the drum hits there was no other instrument playing. All of the information was in the tail of each hit, which is the quietest part of the quietest thing in the file. I am going to play you ten seconds of it now, at exactly the level it shipped at. The playhead crosses the chart in real time, and every shaded stripe is a moment where the two settings genuinely differ. Watch the stripes go past and notice how little arrives at your ears.

Now the same two files with fourteen decibels of gain added to both of them. One number, applied to each equally, so nothing between them has moved — the difference is exactly as big as it was a moment ago, it is simply somewhere you can reach it. Listen to how long each hit rings on after it is struck. That is the whole of case two, and here is the sentence I want you to keep. A difference in decibels is not a difference you can hear. Before you trust a comparison, ask what absolute level it is happening at, not just how big it is. A gap of eleven decibels between two whispers in another room is a perfectly real gap and you will never hear it. The measurement was never wrong. It answered the question it was asked — how far apart are these two things — and that was not the question that mattered. The question that mattered was whether a person could hear it, and nothing in the whole pipeline was measuring that. The real fix, for the record, was not to make it louder. It was to change the material, so that something was playing underneath the drums for the compressor to push down and let back up.

Case three. Look at the bottom right corner of this video. There is a small display down there with a lot of thin vertical lines in it, moving with the sound. It is a real analysis, not a decoration: each line is one slice of the frequency range, and its height is how much energy the film's own audio has in that slice at that instant. Low notes on the left, high notes on the right. It used to have forty-eight of those lines, and the slices are spaced the way we hear, which means they get narrower and narrower towards the bottom. Underneath, the analysis that feeds it can only tell one frequency from another in steps of fifteen hertz. So at the very bottom the slices become narrower than fifteen hertz. And a slice narrower than the step size can end up containing no measurement at all. Not a small measurement. None. The code averaged the nothing it had, got zero, and drew a bar of height zero, every frame, forever. Five of the forty-eight were like that, at roughly thirty-six, forty-one, fifty-three, sixty-eight and ninety-eight hertz. Which is, more or less exactly, the octave a bass guitar lives in — and several of the lessons this meter appeared in were about bass. It was drawing silence precisely where the subject of the video was. And it looked completely fine. Five short bars among forty-eight, at the quiet end where you expect short bars.

There is a second trap hiding inside that one, and it is worth thirty seconds because it is a whole category. When I went to count the broken bars, there were two things I could have counted, and they sound like the same thing. How many slices are narrower than the step size? Eleven. How many slices actually contain no measurement? Five. Both numbers are correct. They are answers to different questions, and only one of them is the fault, because a narrow slice can still happen to have a measurement land inside it. If I had counted the first one I would have gone and corrected a figure that was already right. The comment in the code and the note in the design document say different numbers to this day, and they are both true. Which brings me to case four, and this one is the reason I wanted to make this part at all. In these videos I sometimes put two versions of a sound next to each other — before and after — with a badge on the screen telling you which is which. There is an automatic check that looks at the finished film and makes sure the two halves really are different. Listen to this one.
And now the after. Same passage, same place in the song, same badge in the corner telling you which half you are listening to. Have a listen, and see whether you can tell me what changed.

They were the same file. Not similar. The same samples, played to you twice, and I did that on purpose, just now, so you would have the experience of a demonstration that did not happen. That is not a hypothetical. It shipped. On a real film, a chapter's before and after both pointed at one audio file, and the automatic check measured the difference in loudness between the two halves and reported plus zero point zero zero. Green. Passed. And it was right. That is the part that should bother you. Two identical halves genuinely do not differ in loudness, so a check that measures the difference in loudness will always pass them, correctly, by its own logic, forever. The check was not broken. The check was answering a question that could not distinguish the good case from the catastrophic one. A human noticed, by reading a file that listed which audio each half used. Its sibling is even better. There is another check that is supposed to notice if a video has frozen — if it is really just one still picture for ten minutes. The original version pulled out frames and compared their fingerprints, and if the fingerprints were all different, the picture was moving. It passed a film that was a single still image from beginning to end, because video compression adds a tiny amount of noise to every frame, so every fingerprint differs even when every picture is identical. It now compares the pixels themselves, against a measured floor: a still film reads about zero point one one, a real one about five.

Four cases. Let me put them side by side, because the shape is the point, not the details. A search that never ran, printing the same nothing as a search that ran. A measurement that was accurate about the wrong quantity. A meter that drew a real zero from no data. A test that passed a comparison between a thing and itself. In every one of them, something returned a value that had the correct shape. A number where a number belonged. An empty list where a list belonged. Nothing anywhere raised its hand. And in every one of them, the value it returned was the value I was expecting, which is why I stopped looking. That is the thing I would most want a person who has never written a line of code to take away from this project. It is not that programs break. Everybody knows programs break. It is that the most expensive failures do not feel like failures at all — they feel like progress. You get an answer, you write it down, you build the next thing on top of it, and several days later something a long way away makes no sense and you have no idea why. Every one of these four ended the same way, and it was never a bug where anyone was looking. The instrument was pointed at the wrong thing.

One more, and this one is short, and it is the best of the lot. In that same compressor lesson I wanted to put a number on how fast the effect was letting go of the sound. So I measured how often the level went up and down. Six point four five times a second. A real measurement, from real audio. I put it on a card. Then I measured the slow setting, which should have been obviously different. Six point four five. Then I measured it with the compressor switched off entirely. Six point four five. The number was completely real. It was the drum pattern. I had built an instrument that measured how often the music went up and down, pointed it at some music, and read back the tempo of the music. The figure was retracted. What replaced it is arithmetic instead of a comparison: the effect's own recovery time can be predicted from its settings before you render anything, and the prediction and the measurement now agree to about a fiftieth of a millisecond. Notice what saved it, though. Not cleverness. The control. Measuring the case where the answer had to be different, and finding that it was not.

So that is part three. The characteristic failure of this project is not a crash. It is a wrong answer wearing the costume of a right one, and the defence against it is not talent, it is a habit. Prove the instrument can find a thing that is there before you believe it when it says nothing is. Distrust a zero that came out of something you built yourself half an hour ago. When two instruments disagree, that disagreement is the most useful thing you own that day. And a number that never changes, no matter what you do to it, is not a measurement of anything. There are a hundred and forty-eight separate checking scripts in this project, and the reason there are that many is everything I have just described. Which leaves one question, and it is the one part four is about. If a test can pass while the thing it tests does not exist, then what exactly does a green light buy you? The answer turns out to be more interesting than the question. You break the thing on purpose, and you check that the test goes red. A test that has never been seen to fail is not evidence of anything at all. Thank you for watching.

description:
Part three of a series about building a digital audio workstation from nothing. The real enemy was never a crash — a crash tells you. It was a wrong answer that looks exactly like a right one. Four documented cases from this project's own record.

THE CODE WAS WRITTEN BY AN AI AGENT WORKING WITH ONE PERSON.

THE FOUR CASES, WITH THE COMMANDS THAT RE-DERIVED THEM
1. A search wrapped in a command this machine does not have, with its error redirected away: exit 127, 0 bytes of output — indistinguishable from a search that ran and found nothing. The working command finds 3 files. (Reproduced live in this build; the thrown-away error was "bash: timeout: command not found".)
2. A compressor demonstration measured at 11.5 dB apart, living at -39.9 vs -51.5 dBFS. Re-measured here from the two wavs that actually shipped: mean gap 7.0 dB, widest 12.8 dB, at about -41 dBFS — roughly 25 dB below this film's own level, and 73% of the excerpt is digital silence in both. Both files are played verbatim, then again with ONE shared static gain of 14 dB on both halves (the A/B relationship is asserted unchanged to 2.5e-07 dB).
3. 48 log-spaced meter bands against a 15 Hz analysis grid: 5 contain no analysis line at all and drew a permanent zero, at 36.2, 41.0, 52.6, 67.5, 98.2 Hz. ⚠ 11 bands are NARROWER than one line — a different question with a different answer. After the fix, 0 are dead (docs/research/design-lesson-rebuild.md, scripts/video/meter.py).
4. An A/B check whose two halves resolved to one file passed at +0.00 LU, correctly by its own logic; and a frame check that hashed PNGs passed a film that was a single still image. Pixel floor now 0.11 still vs 5.04 real (CHANGELOG.md, plugins/narrated-film/scripts/verify.py).

BONUS: a "pumping rate" measured at 6.45 Hz on the fast setting, 6.45 on the slow one and 6.45 with the effect bypassed. It was the drum pattern. Retracted, and replaced with a prediction: 74.55 / 248.49 / 1987.93 ms predicted, 74.57 / 248.49 / 1987.92 measured.

SCALE: 148 gate scripts, 105 commits between 2026-07-06 and 2026-09-04.

DISCLOSURE
The narration is a synthetic voice, generated locally. No music-generation model was used: every note in the demo track was written by hand and played by the application's own sound bank. The A/B in chapter nine is DELIBERATELY the same file on both sides — that is the demonstration.
